name: Omar Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Can you describe a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Omar Usman, 27, a senior lineworker and crew lead. We meet near the rail-side service yard, check the outage map on a tablet, and head out to replace hardware or clear faults; I usually take the first climb if the crew is new to the site.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you most enjoy, and what is hardest on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like working with my hands and getting a repair done before the evening load picks up. The travel and weather can be rough, but I earn typical pay and have a few months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the app can sort yesterday’s outage list, but it can’t tell if a conductor is rubbing a branch until someone checks the span. I’m happy to use a quicker report if the crew still verifies it outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work and pay stay much the same with a small tool like that. I already use AI to look up equipment manuals, and my savings mean I can handle an ordinary repair bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the app’s list against the crew’s inspection notes for several shifts, then use it if the reports agree. I’d keep my normal route and savings transfer instead of buying extra software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because the tool handles a small office task, not the climb. I still want a person to confirm a hazard before we touch the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What detail would make you reject the app’s report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d reject it if the address, pole number or crew notes didn’t match the route sheet. A clean-looking screen is not enough when it sends us to live equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your own money to get a better app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the company should choose and pay for work software. I’d keep my own savings for household bills and the next vehicle service.

say: I’d say an app can sort **outage lists**, but crews must inspect the span.
I’d use faster reports only when **field checks agree**.
think: I think my work and pay stay **mostly the same** in this small change.
I can manage an ordinary bill with **a few months saved**.
do: Compare app reports with **inspection notes** for several shifts.
Keep the **normal route** and savings transfer.
Use only company-approved **work software** paid for by the employer.
feel: I feel **calm**, because this tool does not touch the climb.
S0.quote: A clean-looking screen is not enough when it sends us to live equipment.
fieldNote: Omar is comfortable trying software but keeps **hazard confirmation** with workers who inspect the site in person.
His typical pay and **moderate savings** make the limited change manageable.

steps.text: Compare app reports against inspection notes on several shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI can schedule work and order fittings, but it should show the crew why a job is prioritized. I’d rather spend the saved office time inspecting older spans than rush through another set of forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of my team-lead planning could be done by the system, so I may lose part of the role. I’m comfortable learning tools, but I know faster planning could mean fewer paid lead hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the scheduling interface early and run it beside the old route board to find errors. I’d ask for more field inspections and save overtime while I see what the company does with lead posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because a reduction in lead hours would reach my household, though I have some savings and can act early. I don’t think learning the tool makes me immune to fewer positions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the system to show when it assigns a crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the reason for the call-out, the access restriction and the hardware the crew needs. If the system gives a recommendation without its basis, I’d check with dispatch before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply elsewhere now, or wait to see whether hours change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d wait for the company’s actual staffing plan before applying, since I have a few months of savings and some nearby employers. If a real lead vacancy opened, then I’d compare its duties and pay.

say: I’d say AI can schedule work, but it should explain **job priorities**.
I’d use saved office time for **span inspections**.
think: I think the system could take some **lead planning duties**.
Learning the tool will not protect me if **lead hours shrink**.
do: Learn the **scheduling interface** beside the old route board.
Ask for more **field inspections** and save overtime pay.
Wait for the company’s **staffing plan** before applying elsewhere.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because fewer lead hours could affect my household.
S1.quote: I don’t think learning the tool makes me immune to fewer positions.
fieldNote: He adopts tools early but sees **planning as vulnerable**, including his lead hours.
He uses his savings to **wait for staffing news**, not to assume security.

steps.text: Learn the scheduling interface beside the current route board
Continue field inspections with the crew
Save overtime pay while lead hours remain steady
Wait for the published staffing plan before applying elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say planning, ordering, records and fault diagnosis are not protected after 2028. We have roughly three years before the robot date, and the company should use that time to explain what happens to field crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead planning could be automated quickly, and the physical work could be challenged in 2031. My savings give me a short period to adjust, but I’d expect some real risk to my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take a practical electrical safety trainer course before 2028 and ask my employer to pay for it. In 2029 I’d apply for trainer or inspection vacancies, checking each one because teaching, records and diagnosis can also be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing lead hours and then having robots reach the field work. I can take a course and use my savings, but neither one promises that a vacancy will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about the training plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say I want to use paid time for a course before we spend our savings on it. We’d keep our current budget until I knew whether a real opening existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could trainer work protect you after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t assume it will; the system can make lesson plans and diagnose faults as well. I’d consider it only if there were a real position and would keep checking how the hands-on work changes before 2031.

say: I’d say planning and diagnosis are **not protected after 2028**.
I’d ask how the company will use the **three years before robots**.
think: I think my **lead planning** could be automated quickly.
My savings give me time, but I expect a real **income risk**.
do: Take a practical **electrical safety trainer course** before 2028.
Apply for actual trainer or inspection vacancies in **2029** and check duties.
Keep **household spending** steady until a real opening appears.
feel: I feel **anxious about income**, with a few actions but no guaranteed vacancy.
S2.quote: My savings give me a short period to adjust, but I’d expect some real risk to my income.
fieldNote: Omar expects exposure in **lead planning** and later line work, not a guaranteed transfer to another position.
He pursues a course while recognizing **trainer tasks** also involve thinking work.

steps.text: Complete a practical electrical safety trainer course before 2028
Apply to actual trainer or inspection vacancies in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to prepare and keep the safety side in view. I would still expect AGI to take planning in 2031, with robots reaching the line work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have more time than in the 2028 picture to build savings and try a course while I’m earning. I still think my lead duties could shrink, and inspection roles may not last once AGI can diagnose faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get a recognized trainer qualification and verify what jobs it connects to before I commit. In 2032 I’d apply to actual openings, and I’d only consider moving if the wages covered rent and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years gives me time to prepare without spending my savings in a rush. I have some nearby employers, yet I’d still need a real offer before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test whether the course is worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check the qualification name with the employer and speak to someone already doing the trainer job. I’d ask how much of that work is practical and how much is lesson writing or diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start applying immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d first finish enough of the course to show what I can do, then apply where the vacancy and pay are clear. I won’t move on a rumor about future hiring.

say: I’d say five years gives us time to prepare and **check safety procedures**.
I expect planning to change in 2031 and line work to face robots in **2034**.
think: I have time to build savings and **study while earning**.
I think my **lead duties and diagnosis** may shrink as AGI arrives.
do: Verify a **recognized trainer qualification** and its related jobs.
Apply for real vacancies in **2032** after completing course work.
Move only when **written wages** cover rent and travel.
feel: I feel **anxious but more prepared**, with savings and time to check offers.
S3.quote: I’m anxious, but five years gives me time to prepare without spending my savings in a rush.
fieldNote: He uses the longer runway to **verify training value**, not rush into a new field.
Nearby employers help, but he wants **confirmed pay before moving**.

steps.text: Verify the trainer qualification with the employer

Continue savings while completing the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade lets us test training, save money and ask for a clear plan from the employer. I’d still expect records and diagnosis to change by 2036, with robots reaching the field work in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can prepare in stages and keep most of my savings while I learn what jobs exist. I won’t treat trainer or inspection work as protected, because AI can take the planning and diagnosis too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take a practical trainer course over time and keep putting money into my emergency fund. In 2037 I’d check actual job duties and pay, and apply only if a vacancy was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed than with two years, and my savings give me a base for a move if it makes sense. I’m still uneasy because a decade doesn’t guarantee the next job or stop the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner see you do differently this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She’d see me reserve an evening for the course and keep our savings transfer steady. We’d wait to move until I had a job offer with enough pay to cover the new rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a trainer job be a safe career after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, lesson planning and fault diagnosis are thinking work, so that job could change too. I’d treat it as one possible role to investigate and keep my savings for an uncertain transition.

say: I’d say a decade lets us test training and **request an employer plan**.
I expect records to change in 2036 and field work in **2039**.
think: I can prepare in stages and keep **most of my savings**.
I won’t call trainer or inspection work **protected** after AGI.
do: Take a practical **trainer course** over time.
Keep adding money to my **emergency fund**.
Check actual duties and pay in **2037** before applying.
feel: I feel **less rushed**, while still uncertain about the next job.
S4.quote: I’m still uneasy because a decade doesn’t guarantee the next job or stop the robot date.
fieldNote: A longer warning allows **staged learning and saving**, not a guarantee of stable work.
He expects **trainer tasks to change** and delays moving until a real offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it leaves only three years before robots arrive and gives little time to adjust my lead work. Paid training, clear information about crew numbers and a list of real openings would help me make decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is responsible when a system sends a crew to the wrong place or leaves out a hazard. I like using tools that save time, but the employer still has to own the safety result.

headlineQuote: I like using tools that save time, but the employer still has to own the safety result.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old senior lineworker** who leads crews and enjoys practical repairs.
He earns typical pay and has **a few months saved**.
He adopts useful technology early but keeps **field safety checks** in human hands.
He uses warning time to **train and save**, while acknowledging the next role may also change.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time before robots arrive and lead work changes.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, clear crew information and a list of real openings would help him decide.
